title: The Endless Room
premise: Coral Sterling takes a teaching post at Marrow Creek School, where an entire class vanished in 1974 and the staff maintain strange rituals—counting doors, keeping lights burning—to keep something at bay. When her mirrors begin lagging a second behind reality, she discovers the missing students were pulled into 'the endless room,' a mirrored space sustained by a song whose final verse was never written down, because singing it completes the trap. As Coral bonds with the school's ragtag survivors and the ghost-children still echoing inside the glass, she learns the last verse can only be learned by entering the room itself—without ever singing along. In the climax she faces her own reflection wearing her face and offering her everything she's lost; by refusing to sing, she breaks the loop, frees the children, and chooses her found family over the false self in the glass.
about_author: P. M. Okonkwo is the pen name of a former night-shift teacher who swears every school has one door that shouldn't be counted twice. They write horror about ordinary people who refuse to look away from the thing looking back.

chapters.title: The Door Count
chapters.summary: POV Coral. On her first day at Marrow Creek School, Coral notices the janitor counting doors aloud each evening and the principal's rule: never let a hallway go dark. A student, Wren, whispers that Room 12 has no students but is always warm. The beat is quiet unease—the sense that everyone knows something they've agreed not to say.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Digging through the archive, Coral finds a class photo: twenty-eight smiling children, all listed as 'transferred' on the same October day. The custodian, Amos, admits the class walked into Room 12 during a fire drill and never came out. The emotional beat is the first crack in Coral's skepticism—grief disguised as bureaucracy.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV Coral. At home, Coral's bathroom mirror reflects her raising a hand before she does it—or after; the timing is off by exactly one second. She tests it with a coin, a match, a scream. The beat is escalating dread as the lag widens to two seconds, then three, and her reflection begins moving when she doesn't.

chapters.title: The Song
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Wren hums a skipping rhyme in class and every light in the wing flickers; Amos slams the piano lid shut. He explains the endless room is held open by the song, sung in rounds by whoever is inside—and the last verse, the one that seals it forever, exists only in the room. Beat: loyalty tested, as Amos begs Coral to leave before she hears too much.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Coral, Wren, Amos, and nurse Delphine form a fragile pact over burnt dinners and shared research, mapping every mirror in town that lags. Wren confesses her sister was in the 1974 photo. The beat is warmth against horror—the found family forming precisely because the truth is unbearable alone.

chapters.title: What the Glass Keeps
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Shifting to Wren's POV, she touches the lagging mirror in the girls' restroom and sees her sister, older, mouthing the song's opening lines. Wren nearly sings along; Coral pulls her back. The beat is temptation—the room offers reunion, and grief makes everyone a willing door.

chapters.title: The Pull
chapters.summary: POV Coral. The mirrors stop lagging and start leading: Coral's reflection walks out of frame. That night her whole house becomes glass, and she is drawn through into the endless room—a corridor of doors, each opening onto October 1974. Beat: terror and terrible beauty as she realizes she chose to come, on some level, all along.

chapters.title: The Children of Room Twelve
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Inside, Coral meets the lost class, unaged, singing in rounds to keep the room from consuming them. They teach her the verses up to the penultimate line and warn her: the last verse is a lie tailored to the listener. Her own reflection appears, wearing her mother's voice. Beat: compassion sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Coral, climax. The reflection offers Coral the life she mourns—her old name, her old family—if she sings the closing verse. Around her, the children begin to falter as the song loses its round. Coral learns the true last verse is silence, and holds it while the room tears itself apart trying to make her speak. Beat: sacrifice without martyrdom.

chapters.title: Counting Forward
chapters.summary: POV Coral, resolution. Coral wakes on the school floor with twenty-eight children and no mirrors anywhere lagging. Room 12 is cold for the first time in fifty years. The found family counts the doors together—not to keep something out, but to mark what came home. Final beat: quiet hope, and one mirror, covered, left deliberately unbroken.
